title: Modules
summary: **Modules** let you split TypeScript code into files that explicitly `export` and `import` what they share. TS adds *type-only imports*, *re-exports/barrels*, and supports legacy *namespaces* alongside ambient module declarations.

subtopics.title: ES module import/export
subtopics.explanation: Any file with a top-level import or export is a module: its declarations are private unless exported. You expose values with export and pull them in with import. This is the standard JS module system that TypeScript builds on, replacing global script scope with explicit dependencies.
subtopics.example:
export function add(a: number, b: number) { return a + b; }
import { add } from './math';

subtopics.title: Named vs default exports
subtopics.explanation: Named exports (export const x) are imported by their exact name in braces and can have many per file. A default export (export default) is the file's single primary export, imported under any name without braces. Teams often prefer named exports because they are explicit, refactor-friendly, and tree-shake well.

subtopics.title: Module resolution
subtopics.explanation: Module resolution is how TypeScript turns a specifier like './math' or 'lodash' into an actual file. Relative paths resolve against the importing file; bare specifiers resolve from node_modules. The moduleResolution setting (node/node16/bundler) controls the algorithm and whether file extensions are required.
subtopics.example:
import { x } from './sub/util';   // relative
import _ from 'lodash';           // from node_modules

subtopics.title: Type-only imports (import type)
subtopics.explanation: import type imports a symbol purely for its type, guaranteeing the import is erased from the emitted JavaScript. This avoids accidental runtime dependencies and side effects, and is required under isolatedModules/verbatimModuleSyntax when a symbol is used only as a type.
subtopics.example:
import type { User } from './models';
import { type Role, fetchRole } from './roles';

subtopics.title: Re-exports and barrels
subtopics.explanation: A re-export forwards another module's exports: export { add } from './math' or export * from './math'. A barrel is an index.ts that re-exports a folder's public API so consumers import from one path. Barrels improve ergonomics but can hurt tree-shaking and create circular imports if overused.

subtopics.title: Namespaces (legacy) vs modules
subtopics.explanation: Namespaces (formerly 'internal modules', namespace Foo { ... }) group code under a global object without import/export. They predate ES modules and are now discouraged for application code — prefer ES modules. Namespaces still appear in declaration files and for organizing types in some libraries.
subtopics.example:
namespace Geometry { export const PI = 3.14159; }
console.log(Geometry.PI);

subtopics.title: Ambient modules
subtopics.explanation: An ambient module declaration (declare module 'name') tells TypeScript about a module's types without providing an implementation — used to type untyped packages, non-code imports (CSS, images), or to augment existing modules. It lives in a .d.ts file and is covered in depth under declaration files.

foundations.overview: Modules are how TypeScript organizes code into independent, reusable files with explicit dependencies. A file becomes a module the moment it has a top-level import or export; everything else stays private to that file. On top of standard ES modules, TypeScript layers type-aware features like import type and ambient module declarations, plus a configurable resolution algorithm that maps specifiers to files.
foundations.formalDefinition: A module is a file whose top-level bindings are scoped to the file and shared only via export/import declarations. TypeScript resolves each import specifier to a file using the configured moduleResolution strategy, type-checks the imported symbols, and emits JavaScript modules according to the module compiler option.
foundations.whyItMatters: Modules are the unit of code organization in every real TypeScript project. Understanding named vs default exports, resolution, and type-only imports is essential for clean architecture, correct builds, and good tree-shaking — and it is a frequent interview topic because misuse causes circular dependencies and bloated bundles.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each file as a sealed box: nothing leaks out unless you export it, and nothing comes in unless you import it. import type is a label on the box saying 'types only — discard at runtime.' A barrel is a reception desk that forwards visitors to the right inner office.
foundations.browserPerspective: Browsers run native ES modules via <script type="module">. TypeScript's module option decides what is emitted — ESM (esnext) ships modern import/export the browser understands, while commonjs is for Node. Type-only imports vanish entirely, so the browser never downloads code for symbols used only as types.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every feature folder exports its public API, shared utilities live in a lib/ module, and barrels (index.ts) provide tidy import paths. Type-only imports keep model files from pulling runtime code, and ambient modules let projects import CSS/SVG or untyped packages.
foundations.businessImpact: Well-structured modules speed onboarding and feature delivery: developers find and reuse code quickly, and correct module/resolution settings keep bundles small, which improves load times and conversion.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Explicit module boundaries make dependencies visible, enable code splitting and tree-shaking, and prevent the tangled global scope of script-era code. Type-only imports and isolatedModules keep builds fast and predictable.
foundations.performanceImpact: Module shape directly affects bundle size. Named exports and avoiding heavy barrels improve tree-shaking; type-only imports remove dead runtime dependencies. Circular imports from sloppy barrels can cause runtime ordering bugs and slow builds.
commonUseCases: Splitting features into files with explicit public APIs
Barrel files (index.ts) for clean import paths
Type-only imports to keep model files runtime-free
Ambient module declarations for CSS/SVG or untyped packages

commonMisconceptions.myth: A default export is better or faster than named exports.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Defaults are just one export per file; named exports are more explicit, refactor-friendly, and usually tree-shake better. Neither is faster at runtime.

commonMisconceptions.myth: import type is the same as a regular import.
commonMisconceptions.reality: import type is guaranteed to be erased from the output, so it never creates a runtime dependency or triggers side effects — a normal import may.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Namespaces and ES modules are interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Namespaces are a legacy global-grouping feature; modern app code should use ES modules. Namespaces mainly survive in declaration files.

debuggingLab.title: Default import name mismatch
debuggingLab.symptom: A default-exported value is imported using braces (named-import syntax), so the symbol is undefined at runtime.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A default export has no exported name — import { log } looks for a *named* export called log, which does not exist, so log is undefined and calling it throws. The default must be imported without braces under a chosen name.
commonMistakes: Using braces to import a default export.
Mixing up export default with export const when importing.
Assuming the import name must match the export (it does for named, not for default).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Import the default export correctly (no braces) and call it.

theory.question: What makes a TypeScript file a module, and how do named and default exports differ?
theory.directAnswer: A file becomes a module as soon as it has a top-level import or export — its declarations then become private and are shared only through exports. Named exports (export const x) can be many per file and are imported by exact name in braces; a default export is the single primary export, imported under any name without braces. Teams often prefer named exports because they are explicit and refactor-friendly.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Module scope is per-file isolation where bindings are private unless exported; exports come in named and default flavors.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To replace the global script scope of early JS with explicit, reusable dependencies and clear public APIs.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler treats any file with top-level import/export as a module, type-checks the exported/imported symbols, and emits the configured module format.

theory.whyImportant: Module structure underpins all real codebases; confusing named and default imports is a classic source of 'undefined' bugs and bad refactors.
theory.realWorldExample: A models.ts file exports named types and a service.ts exports a default service class; consumers import them with the right syntax for each.

nestedTopics.title: Module vs script
nestedTopics.explanation: Without any top-level import/export, a file is a global script and its declarations leak into global scope.

nestedTopics.title: Tree-shaking
nestedTopics.explanation: Named exports generally tree-shake better than barrels with side effects.

followUps.question: Why might a team ban default exports?
followUps.answer: Default exports can be imported under any name, which hurts grep-ability and consistent renaming; named exports keep one canonical identifier.

theory.question: What is `import type`, and why does it exist?
theory.directAnswer: import type imports a symbol purely for use as a type, and TypeScript guarantees that import is erased from the emitted JavaScript. It exists to prevent accidental runtime dependencies and side effects, and it is required under flags like isolatedModules/verbatimModuleSyntax when a symbol is used only as a type so the transpiler can safely drop it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A type-only import declaration that never produces runtime code.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So single-file transpilers (Babel, esbuild) can erase type imports without whole-program analysis, and to avoid importing runtime code you only needed for typing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler flags the import as type-only and omits it from the output; you can also mark individual specifiers with the inline type keyword.

theory.whyImportant: Misunderstanding it causes either runtime errors under isolatedModules or unintended runtime imports and side effects.
theory.realWorldExample: import type { User } from './models' in a component avoids pulling any runtime code from the models file that also exports values.

nestedTopics.title: Inline type
nestedTopics.explanation: import { type Role, fetchRole } mixes a type-only and a value import in one statement.

nestedTopics.title: verbatimModuleSyntax
nestedTopics.explanation: A modern flag that enforces type-only imports be written explicitly.

followUps.question: Can a type-only import cause a side effect?
followUps.answer: No — it is erased entirely, so any module side effects on import never run for a type-only import.

scenario.question: Your app's bundle ballooned after the team added a big barrel index.ts that re-exports everything, and you're seeing occasional circular-dependency warnings. How do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Stop importing the whole feature through the mega-barrel. Import directly from the specific module, split the barrel into smaller, side-effect-free re-exports, and break cycles by moving shared types/constants into a leaf module that both sides import. Use export type for type-only re-exports and ensure the barrel has no runtime side effects so tree-shaking can drop unused exports.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A diagnosis of barrel-induced bundle bloat and circular imports.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single index.ts that re-exports an entire feature forces bundlers to pull in (and order) everything, defeating tree-shaking and creating import cycles.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Direct imports and leaf modules for shared types remove the central hub that creates cycles and unnecessary coupling.

scenario.whyImportant: Bundle size and circular dependencies are real production problems that trace directly back to module organization choices.

nestedTopics.title: Tree-shaking
nestedTopics.explanation: Side-effect-free, named re-exports let bundlers drop unused code.

nestedTopics.title: Breaking cycles
nestedTopics.explanation: Extract shared types/constants to a dependency-free leaf module.

followUps.question: How can sideEffects help?
followUps.answer: Marking the package's "sideEffects": false in package.json lets bundlers safely prune unused barrel re-exports.

coding.question: Design a small barrel module: given math and string utility modules, write the index that re-exports a clean public API including a type-only re-export.
coding.thoughtProcess: A barrel forwards exports without re-implementing them. I'll use export { ... } from for selected named values, export * from when forwarding all, and export type { ... } from for type-only symbols so they are erased at runtime. The consumer then imports everything from the single barrel path.
coding.lineByLine: export { add } from './math' forwards a single named value; export type { Vec2 } from './math' forwards only the type, guaranteed erased; export * from './strings' forwards every named export of strings. The consumer imports values and types from the one barrel path.
coding.spaceComplexity: N/A — no extra runtime allocation; type re-exports are erased.

alternativeApproaches.title: No barrel (direct imports)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Importing each symbol directly from its source avoids cycles and improves tree-shaking at the cost of more verbose import paths.
alternativeApproaches.code:
// import { add } from './math';
// import { upper } from './strings';

followUps.question: Why use export type instead of export in a barrel?
followUps.answer: export type guarantees the re-exported symbol is type-only and erased, so the barrel never adds a runtime dependency for a pure type.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Modules define the dependency graph of an app. A common shape is feature folders that each expose a small public API (often via a thin barrel), shared lib/ utilities, and a types/ layer imported with import type. The module and moduleResolution options align this graph with the target runtime (ESM for browsers/bundlers, CommonJS for legacy Node).
productionDeepDive.performance: Module choices drive bundle size: prefer named exports and avoid side-effectful barrels so bundlers can tree-shake. Type-only imports remove dead runtime dependencies. Deep barrel chains and circular imports slow builds and can cause runtime initialization-order bugs.
productionDeepDive.security: Modules themselves are organizational, but resolution matters: misconfigured paths or trusting arbitrary dynamic import specifiers can load unintended code. Keep third-party imports explicit and audited; never build import paths from untrusted input.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As codebases grow, enforce module boundaries (lint rules like no-restricted-imports, import/no-cycle) so features depend only on intended public APIs. Move shared types/constants to leaf modules to prevent cycles.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Consistent export style (favor named exports), small focused barrels, and import type for type-only usage keep the dependency graph readable and refactors safe. Tools can auto-fix import ordering and detect cycles.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit in CI catches resolution and type errors; bundlers report module sizes and circular-dependency warnings. Source maps preserve module structure for debugging emitted code.

caseStudies.problem: Apps shipped far more JavaScript than needed because everything was reachable through global scope or giant barrels.
caseStudies.solution: ES modules with named exports, sideEffects flags, and tree-shaking remove unused code at build time.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Requires discipline (avoid side-effectful modules) and correct module settings, but yields dramatically smaller bundles.
caseStudies.lessons: Module boundaries and export style are a first-class performance and maintainability concern, not just organization.

keyTakeaways: A file is a module once it has a top-level import or export; otherwise it is a global script.
Named exports are imported by exact name in braces; a default export is imported under any name without braces.
import type is guaranteed to be erased at runtime, preventing accidental dependencies and side effects.
Module resolution (controlled by moduleResolution) maps specifiers to files; relative paths resolve locally, bare specifiers from node_modules.
Barrels improve import ergonomics but can hurt tree-shaking and cause cycles; namespaces are legacy — prefer ES modules.
